data.title: Phrynoderma — viva
data.summary: Nutritional & metabolic · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Phrynoderma** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What is phrynoderma?**
- 'Toad skin' — follicular hyperkeratotic papules with a central keratotic plug, classically linked to vitamin A deficiency but now considered a marker of multiple nutritional deficiencies (vitamin A, B-complex, E, essential fatty acids, protein-energy malnutrition)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Dry rough skin with symmetric, firm, skin-coloured to brown follicular papules (2–6 mm) with central horny spines; first on extensor elbows, knees, then thighs, buttocks, shoulders, extensor forearms, back
- School-age children commonest, especially in low-income settings; may coexist with xerophthalmia (night blindness, Bitot's spots, xerosis conjunctivae, keratomalacia), angular cheilitis, glossitis

**Q3. Discuss features of vitamin A deficiency and hypervitaminosis A (PYQ).**
- Deficiency: xerosis, phrynoderma, hair dryness, night blindness (earliest), conjunctival/corneal xerosis, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia, increased infections (measles severity)
- Hypervitaminosis A (acute — polar bear liver, mega-doses; chronic — retinoid excess): headache, raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumour cerebri), vomiting; skin — dryness, peeling, cheilitis, alopecia, pruritus, hyperpigmentation; bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, hypercalcaemia, teratogenicity

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Follicular hyperkeratosis with keratotic plugs distending the follicle, atrophy of sebaceous glands, mild perifollicular infiltrate

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Keratosis pilaris (outer arms/thighs, atopic, finer, lifelong), lichen spinulosus (grouped spiny papules in plaques), pityriasis rubra pilaris (knuckle papules, orange keratoderma), Darier's disease (greasy seborrhoeic papules), follicular eczema, lichen nitidus, scurvy (perifollicular haemorrhage + corkscrew hair), frictional lichenoid eruption, follicular mucinosis

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Serum retinol (<20 µg/dl deficiency), CBC, total protein/albumin, other vitamins/zinc as indicated; eye examination
- Clinical response to supplementation supports diagnosis

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Vitamin A: WHO therapy for xerophthalmia — 2 lakh IU (200,000 IU) orally on day 1, day 2 and after 2 weeks (1 lakh IU for 6–12 months, 50,000 IU <6 months)
- Balanced diet with green leafy vegetables, yellow/orange fruits, dairy; B-complex, vitamin E, essential fatty acid (safflower oil) supplements; treat underlying malnutrition, malabsorption
- Topical keratolytics: urea 10–20%, salicylic acid, lactic acid; emollients
- National programme: biannual vitamin A prophylaxis for children 9 months–5 years (India)

**Q8. Discuss skin changes in kwashiorkor (PYQ).**
- Protein deficiency with adequate calories (1–5 y after weaning): 'flaky-paint' / 'crazy-pavement' dermatosis (hyperpigmented patches that peel leaving pink/hypopigmented areas), especially pressure areas, buttocks and legs
- Hair: dry, sparse, easily pluckable, hypopigmented (reddish-brown), 'flag sign' (alternating bands of light and dark hair indicating periods of poor and good nutrition)
- Oedema (pitting), moon face, hepatomegaly (fatty liver), apathy, growth failure; marasmus: wasting, loose wrinkled skin, 'monkey facies', no oedema

**Q9. Describe Bitot's spots and xerophthalmia staging (WHO).**
- XN night blindness, X1A conjunctival xerosis, X1B Bitot's spots (foamy triangular grey-white patches on temporal bulbar conjunctiva), X2 corneal xerosis, X3A/B corneal ulceration/ keratomalacia, XS corneal scar, XF xerophthalmic fundus

**Q10. Why is vitamin A important for skin?**
- Retinoic acid regulates epidermal differentiation (keratin expression), sebaceous gland function and immunity; deficiency → squamous metaplasia and follicular hyperkeratosis; excess → peeling, cheilitis, alopecia

**Q11. What is the role of essential fatty acid deficiency?**
- Linoleic acid deficiency (TPN without lipids, fat malabsorption) causes dry scaly dermatitis, follicular papules, alopecia, poor wound healing — triene:tetraene ratio >0.4; corrected by oral/ IV lipid or topical sunflower/ safflower oil

**Q12. Phrynoderma in adults — causes.**
- Alcoholism, malabsorption (coeliac, Crohn's, chronic pancreatitis, bariatric surgery), chronic liver disease, restrictive diets/ anorexia, HIV

**Q13. Response to treatment.**
- Follicular papules improve over 4–8 weeks with vitamin/ nutritional supplementation and keratolytics; night blindness reverses within days of vitamin A

**Q14. Which other nutrients are linked to phrynoderma?**
- Vitamin B-complex (especially B2, B6), vitamin E, vitamin C and essential fatty acid deficiency, protein-energy malnutrition; in India many cases respond to B-complex and EFA supplementation even with normal vitamin A levels

**Q15. Prevention at the community level.**
- Nutrition education (green leafy vegetables, yellow fruits), mid-day meal programmes, biannual vitamin A supplementation for children (9 months–5 years), deworming, treatment of diarrhoea and infections

## Quick spotter facts
- Toad-like follicular spiny papules on elbows/knees of a malnourished child — phrynoderma
- Flag sign — kwashiorkor hair

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nutritional dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
